n0001.title: Spider Silk
n0001.gist: Spider silk's layered molecular structure gives it an unmatched strength-toughness combination that scientists still cannot fully replicate artificially.
n0001.question: Spider silk — why is it so hard to reproduce artificially despite its extraordinary properties? (a survey of structure, uses, and synthesis attempts)

n0002.title: Introduction
n0002.gist: Spiders spin silk for webs, prey capture, shelter, dispersal, and courtship signaling, varying thickness and stickiness by function, though collecting it in bulk remains hard.
n0002.question: Spider silk — what roles does it play in spider life and why is it difficult to harvest? (overview)

n0003.title: What Spider Silk Is
n0003.gist: Spiders spin protein fibre silk for traps, prey restraint, sensing, nests, suspension and gliding, adjusting thickness and stickiness to each purpose.

n0009.title: Collection and Mating Role
n0009.gist: Spiders sometimes eat their own silk, forcible collection from one spider is possible but mass harvesting like silkworms is impractical, and silk also carries courtship signals and sex pheromones during mating.

n0012.title: Properties
n0012.gist: Silk's layered molecular structure of stiff crystalline segments and stretchy amorphous regions produces a rare combination of strength, stretchiness and stickiness.
n0012.question: Properties — what gives spider silk its combination of strength and toughness? (structural, mechanical, and adhesive traits)

n0013.title: Structural
n0013.gist: Spider silk proteins form repeating hard crystalline blocks within a stretchy amorphous matrix, a hierarchical arrangement, refined by chemical additives, that together produces its distinctive performance.

n0020.title: Web Microstructure
n0020.gist: In an orb web the dragline and radial threads interweave crystalline and helical protein regions while the sticky spiral thread, built from different proteins, lacks any crystalline structure.

n0022.title: Mechanical
n0022.gist: Each silk type is tuned for its job, but dragline silk in particular combines high strength with high stretchiness, giving it exceptional toughness compared to steel or Kevlar.

n0028.title: Measured Mechanical Traits
n0028.gist: Across species, silk's stiffness, strength, density, stretch, heat tolerance and shrinkage in water have each been measured, with specific spiders holding records for stiffness, strength, toughness and stretch.

n0050.title: Adhesive
n0050.gist: A two-part pyriform secretion is spun into attachment discs that set instantly, work indefinitely, biodegrade, and bond with many materials, with the spinnerets controlling the glue's stickiness and durability.

n0053.title: Uses
n0053.gist: A single spider produces up to seven silk types, each matched to a distinct ecological task from trapping prey to mating to dispersal.
n0053.question: Uses — how do spiders deploy different silks for different ecological needs? (a table of uses)

n0054.title: Diversity of Silk Functions
n0054.gist: Spiders alone among silk-producers make multiple silk types per individual, and as spiders evolved over hundreds of millions of years their webs grew from simple tubes to complex orbs.

n0057.title: Table of Silk Uses
n0057.gist: Spiders use silk for capturing and immobilising prey, reproduction, aerial dispersal, food, nest building, guide and drop lines, alarm webs, and pheromone trails.

n0059.title: Silk Types
n0059.gist: Different glands produce distinct silk types—dragline, capture-spiral, egg-sac, wrapping, glue and attachment silks—each matched to a specific structural or adhesive role.
n0059.question: Silk types — which glands produce which silks and what jobs do they perform? (gland-by-gland breakdown)

n0060.title: Gland-to-Function Mapping
n0060.gist: Meeting many ecological needs requires silks with different properties as fibres, structures or glue-like globules, and each type traces to a specific gland suited to its particular use.

n0067.title: Specialised Gland Purposes
n0067.gist: Different glands supply silks for housing, construction, defence, prey capture, egg protection and mobility, including fine gossamer threads used for floating or controlled descent.

n0071.title: Synthesis and Fibre Spinning
n0071.gist: Unlike grown biomaterials, silk is pulled on demand from a liquid protein stored in glands, solidifying into fibre only as it is drawn through a tapering duct under shear stress.
n0071.question: Synthesis and fibre spinning — how does a spider turn liquid protein into solid silk fibre? (gland anatomy and spinning mechanics)

n0072.title: Spinning Process
n0072.gist: Silk forms through pultrusion, pulled rather than pushed, as a fibre is drawn from the spider's body through one or more glands rather than rotated or extruded by force.

n0077.title: Silk Gland Structure
n0077.gist: Proteins secreted in the tail self-assemble into micelles that align, acidify, and lose water while passing through the duct, converting a liquid crystal state into solid helix and sheet structures.

n0082.title: Gland Anatomy
n0082.gist: The gland's tail secretes structural proteins, the ampulla stores silk dope and coating proteins, a funnel narrows the duct, and a tapering duct with a valve controls fibre formation and diameter.

n0091.title: Complete Gland Inventory
n0091.gist: An adult garden cross spider carries hundreds of pyriform, aciniform and other glands numbering in the single digits to hundreds, each type dedicated to attachment, framing, prey-wrapping, eggs or adhesive lines.

n0099.title: Artificial Synthesis
n0099.gist: Replicating spider silk artificially requires both reproducing its liquid feedstock and the precise duct conditions that spin it, and few methods have achieved both at once.
n0099.question: Artificial synthesis — can scientists reproduce both the silk protein and the spinning process outside a spider? (feedstock and geometry approaches)

n0100.title: Feedstock Sources
n0100.gist: Because unspun silk's molecular structure is long and complex, researchers have engineered bacteria, silkworms, goats and plants to produce silk proteins, though results vary widely in strength and stretch.

n0107.title: Spinning Geometry
n0107.gist: Because silk proteins alone cannot form fibre without the right duct shape, researchers have tried syringes, hydrophobic surfaces, self-assembled sheets, microfluidics and electrospinning to mimic natural spinning.

n0121.title: Alternative Forms and Synthetic Products
n0121.gist: Beyond fibres, silk proteins can self-assemble into capsules, nanowires, sheets and membranes for medical uses, while companies and labs worldwide have engineered bacteria, yeast, silkworms, goats and microfluidic devices to manufacture synthetic spider silk commercially.

n0136.title: Research and Human Uses
n0136.gist: Decades of research into spider silk's chemistry and spinning have enabled human applications from ancient woven garments to modern medical, optical and scientific technologies.
n0136.question: Research and human uses — how has scientific understanding of spider silk translated into practical applications? (historical survey)

n0137.title: Research Milestones
n0137.gist: Landmark papers since the 1960s established spider silk's amino acid composition, gene sequence, mechanical behavior, crystalline structure, spinning mechanism, and the first successful bacterial synthesis.

n0140.title: Historical Human Use
n0140.gist: Early attempts to weave spider silk fabric date to 1709, and despite ongoing difficulty producing it at scale it has been used for textiles, armour, medical devices and violin strings.

n0145.title: Medicine and Technology
n0145.gist: Spider silk has served folk medicine as wound dressing, aided nerve regeneration research, provided crosshairs for optical instruments, enabled diffraction experiments and biolenses, and suspended fusion targets during laser ignition.
